summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property setter, then puts Rover through two walks and a charge to show the guard at work. Walking costs 2% of battery per minute, and charging can never push the battery past 100%.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Even inside __init__, assigning to self.battery goes through the property setter rather than storing the value directly, so a pet can never be created with an impossible starting battery.

This decorator makes the method below run every time anything assigns to .battery, which is where the clamping to the 0-100 range happens. Everywhere else in the program you write plain assignment and the validation follows for free.
can_walk is a look-before-you-leap check: it reports whether the pet has the energy for the requested walk without changing anything.
This subtraction is really a read of the getter followed by an assignment through the setter, so the battery drains but can never fall below 0.
Asking can_walk first is what makes the second walk of 50 minutes get refused instead of silently draining Rover to nothing.
Rover is at 65% and asks for 40 more, which would be 105; the setter quietly caps him at 100, which is the whole point of protecting the attribute.
